title: Can My DNA Tell Me How to Exercise? I Tried AlterMe to Find Out
gist: Wired rates AlterMe's $1,299-$1,899 DNA-plus-smart-ring fitness system 8/10 after six months: daily AI workouts keyed to a readiness score helped build habits, but the DNA insights were unremarkable, not clinically validated, and carry privacy concerns. The system is a closed ecosystem pitched against Oura and personal trainers.

insights.claim: AlterMe sells a bundled DNA test, smart ring, app with workouts and nutrition at $1,299 for Essential (three-year membership) or $1,899 for Advanced (deeper DNA analysis, lifetime membership).
insights.speaker: Emily Peck
insights.so_what: A premium, upfront-priced hardware-plus-membership model limits the addressable consumer market.
insights.quote: The entry-level AlterMe Essential plan is $1,299, and the AlterMe Advanced plan is $1,899.

insights.claim: The reviewer rated AlterMe 8/10, finding it convenient and habit-forming but premium priced, with short workouts of five to 40 minutes and unrevelatory DNA results; she notes spending the money on a personal trainer is an alternative.
insights.speaker: Emily Peck
insights.so_what: Value proposition rests on habit-building, not unique DNA insight; price is the main barrier.
insights.quote: It has made me more aware of what I eat and made me feel physically stronger
insights.locator: My journey with AlterMe has generally been

insights.claim: AlterMe acknowledges its DNA-based fitness findings are not clinically validated, and research into genetic influence on athletic performance is still developing, though samples are processed in a CLIA- and CAP-certified US lab.
insights.speaker: Emily Peck
insights.so_what: Consumer genomics fitness claims lack clinical validation, a regulatory and credibility risk.
insights.quote: AlterMe acknowledges that its genetic findings reported through DNA testing have not been clinically validated.
insights.locator: Research into genetic influence on athletic performance

insights.claim: AlterMe says its cardio body-composition assessment uses markers ADRB2 rs1042713 and LPL rs328, and its resistance-training model uses obesity-related variants near FTO, GNPDA2, NEGR1 and SLC39A8.
insights.speaker: Emily Peck
insights.so_what: Relies on common obesity and body-composition markers with modest predictive power individually.
insights.quote: For cardio-related body composition response, the markers in our scientific review are ADRB2 rs1042713 and LPL rs328.

insights.claim: The reviewer's report said strength training best fit her genes, her carbohydrate response was 'lower than average', and she is 'externally motivated to exercise', but she found nothing groundbreaking.
insights.speaker: Emily Peck
insights.so_what: Personalized genetic outputs may feel generic to users, limiting retention.
insights.quote: But despite the personalized insights, I hadn’t discovered anything particularly groundbreaking.
insights.locator: So far, everything was sounding on point.

insights.claim: AlterMe says it destroys samples after testing and keeps extracted DNA for 45 days for quality assurance, but the review flags understandable privacy concerns about handing over DNA data.
insights.speaker: Emily Peck
insights.so_what: Genetic data custody is a regulatory and reputational exposure for consumer wellness companies.
insights.quote: extracted DNA is retained for just 45 days for quality assurance
insights.locator: Is the AlterMe App Worth It?

insights.claim: The AlterMe ring uses PPG sensors, a temperature sensor and an accelerometer to compute a 0-100 Readiness score from HRV, resting heart rate, sleep and activity load, then suggests a workout; it is a more closed ecosystem than Oura's Ring 5, which focuses on tracking and integration with Apple Health.
insights.speaker: Emily Peck
insights.so_what: AlterMe competes on prescriptive workouts rather than open tracking, a differentiation versus Oura.
insights.quote: The key difference is that AlterMe is a more closed ecosystem
insights.locator: This type of health tracking is similar

insights.claim: The reviewer found the readiness score sometimes mismatched how she felt, with high scores after poor sleep, and the ring was bulkier than the Oura Ring 5 and scuffed in a couple of months.
insights.speaker: Emily Peck
insights.so_what: Algorithm accuracy and hardware design are weak points versus incumbents.
insights.quote: the app was telling me that my readiness score was high, which left me feeling a little confused
insights.locator: I trust that the app was recommending

insights.claim: AlterMe deliberately lets users choose workout intensity because biometrics cannot capture soreness, illness, stress or the day's demands and choice helps consistency.
insights.speaker: AlterMe representatives
insights.so_what: Product design favors adherence over strict algorithmic prescription.
insights.quote: “Giving you a choice is also an intentional part of the AlterMe experience,”

insights.claim: The app generates meal and snack ideas referencing DNA and macro targets within 20 seconds and tracks macros, which the reviewer found helpful, while its phone-camera 3D body scan estimating body fat and lean mass felt intrusive to her.
insights.speaker: Emily Peck
insights.so_what: Bundled nutrition and body-composition features broaden stickiness but raise data sensitivity.
insights.quote: I found this feature a little intrusive
